The record:
Write the overview of the executive synopsis for the incident on io-shop below: a short paragraph in plain words, for the people who lead the company rather than the engineers who responded - what happened, how long it lasted, what it cost the business and the people who responded, and how it was resolved.

What a reader saw: Shop pages loaded slowly for shoppers
Why, in plain words: The shop's account page waits for a separate pricing service to work out the shopper's basket total, and it likely has no time limit on that wait, so when the pricing service slowed down the page slowed down too, even though it could have been shown without the total.

Figures:
- How long it lasted: 8m 0s {duration}
- What it cost the shop in takings (estimated by Argus): none {customer_loss}
- Nobody was paged: no on-call incident was linked to this one.

What was done to end it:
- Argus: restarted io-pricing - confirmed
- Argus: proposed a fix, PR #532 - opened as a draft

Name {duration} and {customer_loss} in your overview.
Write no figure yourself - not in digits, not spelled out, and not as a word that sizes it ("a brief outage", "a minor loss", "tripled"). Where a figure goes, write its name, braces and all, and the synopsis writes the figure in.
Say nothing about how the incident was resolved beyond what the list of what was done says: a draft fix has not run, and nothing it would do has happened.
Speak of Argus by name, never as "we", "our" or "us": Argus is the system that responded, and each line of what was done says who did it.
Where you say who was affected, say which ones, as the cause does, or that some were, where it does not say which - never how many, and never all of them, where the cause does not say all.
Keep "likely" on what the cause says is likely, and only there.

Call submit_executive_overview with your overview.

The postmortem it is written from:
Shop pages loaded slowly for shoppers
Incident: HighLatency on io-shop
Date: Nov 11, 2026, 02:21 to 02:29 UTC
Status: Draft. 1 of 6 action items are done.
Written by: Argus Postmortem agent, Nov 11, 2026, 02:57:25 UTC. Not reviewed yet. Each part is as of when the work it reports ended, which the timeline dates; who ended the incident is as of now.
First told: Argus posted in Slack, Nov 11, 2026, 02:27:40 UTC
Ended by: Argus: restarted io-pricing - confirmed, nothing to put back

Summary
The service broke at 02:21 UTC and was back to normal at 02:29 UTC, 8 minutes later. What its alert watches went from 214 ms before it began to 1724 ms at its worst. The shop's takings fell short of the same hours on earlier weeks by no more than those hours vary on their own, if at all. The shop's account page waits for a separate pricing service to work out the shopper's basket total, and it likely has no time limit on that wait, so when the pricing service slowed down the page slowed down too, even though it could have been shown without the total. What Argus did: restarted io-pricing - confirmed, nothing to put back. Argus opened a draft fix, PR #532, for a person to review and merge. io-pricing could slow down again, and io-shop's account pages could slow down with it.

Impact
8m 0s - onset until back to normal
1.1% to 1.1% - error rate, before onset and while broken on average (no rise)
214 ms to 1461 ms - what the alert watches, before onset and while broken on average (worst minute 1724 ms; the rule's line is 600 ms)
none - customer loss (estimated)

Root cause and contributing factors
In the files Code-Fix read, io-shop's account page gets the basket total by calling io-pricing inline through `basket_total`, which waits however long the call takes and sets no time limit. The page already falls back to rendering without the total when the call raises `PricingServiceFailed`, but a slow call never raises, so however long io-pricing took was added straight onto the account page's response time. It rests on F1, a reading of the source nothing ran, so it is unverified.
Causal chain
symptom Shoppers waited longer for io-shop's pages: the slowest requests, the ones the service's high-percentile response time tracks, took far longer than before, while failed requests stayed within their normal range.
  Evidence:
    AL1 p95 latency above threshold for 5m
why 1 io-shop was waiting on io-pricing: from the onset, its calls to io-pricing for a shopper's basket total took about 1500ms each. The log line counted between 88 and 200 such slow requests out of 200 each minute, typically 200.
  Evidence:
    G9feb WARN io-shop: slow upstream call - pricing.io-internal.svc took 1500ms for /v1/shoppers/shopper-#-#-#/basket-total (# of 200 requests) - 7 occurrences in 7 minutes, 02:21–02:27; /v1/shoppers/shopper-#-#-#/basket-total took 7 different values; # was 88 to 200, typically 200, highest at 02:22
    T5 02:28:01 Investigator Agent: Placed the start of the incident at 02:21
    T20 02:31:10 Mitigation Agent: Judged the action CONFIRMED
  Ruled out:
    A deploy, release or flag change on the service: the Investigator Agent asked for production change events - deploys, releases and flag changes on the service, the 1 day 1 minute before Nov 11 02:22; the Investigator Agent read back 0 production changes.
      T7
      T8
    A flag change by anyone but Argus: Argus read the flag provider's history - 0 flag changes by anyone but Argus, the 1 hour before 02:28:06.
      T15
why 2 A slow io-pricing answer slowed the page because the account page calls `basket_total` inline and waits for the basket total with no time limit.
  Evidence:
    F1 What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
    U1 basket_total at src/io_shop/account_page.py:183, in _the_basket_for: calls it: return basket_total(shopper_id, ask_the_pricing_service), None
Contributing factors
- The HighLatency alert on io-shop paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it. (AI-3)
- The record shows no alert on io-pricing's own latency. The slowdown was found only by io-shop's latency alert and then worked out from io-shop's slow-upstream-call log lines. (AI-4)
- io-shop's existing tests of the pricing call use fakes that answer straight away and only report a large `took_ms`, so the tests never exercised a pricing service that actually hangs. (AI-5)

Hypotheses considered
 | Hypothesis | Confidence | Result
C1 | Calls from io-shop to the internal io-pricing service (pricing.io-internal.svc, owned by checkout-platform) began taking about 1500ms from 02:21 UTC. That raised p50 and p95 for the account page. io-shop itself is unchanged: no deploys, a converged rollout, and flat CPU, memory and traffic. | 0.88 | confirmed

Trigger
C1 was confirmed; it blames io-pricing, whose deploys Argus did not read.

Resolution
 | Time (UTC) | Action | By | Kind | Outcome
M1 | 02:28:12 | Restarted io-pricing for C1 | Argus | nothing to put back | confirmed
 | 02:33:06 | Proposed a fix: PR #532 | Code-Fix Agent | nothing to put back | opened as a draft

Detection
The incident on io-shop began at 02:21 UTC. HighLatency fired at 02:27:15 UTC, 6 minutes 15 seconds later.
What the alert said
AL1 | p95 latency above threshold for 5m

Action items
Item | Action | Type | Owner | Tracking | Status
AI-1 | Restarted io-pricing | mitigate | Argus | - | done
AI-2 | Review and merge the proposed fix | prevent | unassigned | PR #532 | open
AI-3 | Route the HighLatency alert on io-shop to an on-call page so a person is told when it fires. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-4 | Add a latency alert on io-pricing's basket-total endpoint, owned by checkout-platform. | detect | unassigned | - | open
AI-5 | Require every call io-shop makes to another service to have a test with a fake service that blocks, checking that the caller returns within a bound. | prevent | unassigned | - | open
AI-6 | Have checkout-platform find out why io-pricing's basket-total calls slowed down from the onset until the restart. | process | unassigned | - | open

Lessons learned
What went well
- The alert came within the 7 minutes 30 seconds accounted for by its rule waiting 5 minutes with its condition holding, its evaluation at intervals of 1 minute, an unmeasured allowance of 30 seconds for scraping and storing its samples and the whole minute the onset is measured to.
- 51 seconds after the alert was raised, the Investigator Agent formed 1 candidate cause, best first: C1.
- 57 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent restarted io-pricing, a dependency of io-shop for C1.
- 3 minutes 55 seconds after the alert was raised, the Mitigation Agent judged the action CONFIRMED.
- 5 minutes 51 seconds after the alert was raised, the Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request - PR #532.
What went wrong
Nothing.
Where it got lucky
- Argus restarted io-pricing without knowing why it had slowed down, and the restart still brought the service back, which kept the slowdown short.

Timeline (UTC)

Response effort
none - engineer time
236,020 - tokens spent by Argus

Supporting information
The incident's walk: http://localhost:8000/incidents/e987f7ac-c1aa-44d7-a33b-5582c079fec6
The fix it proposed: PR #532 (https://github.com/ohadraz/Argus-Demo-Target-App/pull/532) opened as a draft. The record holds nothing about it after that.
Changes to production read
Deploys read, none came back; flags read, none came back.
Log messages read (UTC)
G46bc | ERROR io-shop: account page request failed - ClientDisconnected: the shopper closed the connection - 17 occurrences in 9 minutes, 02:19–02:27
Gbac1 | WARN io-shop: account page error rate at #% over the last minute - 9 occurrences in 9 minutes, 02:19–02:27; # was 0.50% to 2.00%, typically 1.50%, highest at 02:20
G9feb | WARN io-shop: slow upstream call - pricing.io-internal.svc took 1500ms for /v1/shoppers/shopper-#-#-#/basket-total (# of 200 requests) - 7 occurrences in 7 minutes, 02:21–02:27; /v1/shoppers/shopper-#-#-#/basket-total took 7 different values; # was 88 to 200, typically 200, highest at 02:22
What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed - nothing ran its test or its fix
F1 | The fault: in src/io_shop/pricing_service.py, basket_total called ask(shopper_id) inline and waited however long it took. The account page shows the basket total only as a convenience. _the_basket_for in src/io_shop/account_page.py already renders the page without it (pricing_unavailable) when PricingServiceFailed is raised. A slow answer, though, never failed: whatever the pricing call took was added straight onto the page's latency. When io-pricing slowed to about 1500ms, every account page got about 1500ms slower, even though the page could have been shown without that figure. Logging that the call was slow (slow_call) told readers where the time went but did nothing to protect the page.

The change, in src/io_shop/pricing_service.py: basket_total now runs the call on a small module-level thread pool and waits at most budget_ms, which defaults to the new PRICING_BUDGET_MS = 500. If the call has not finished in that time, it cancels the future and raises PricingServiceFailed. The message names the host, the path and the budget. A call still waiting in the pool's queue is cancelled and never runs. A call already running goes on in the background, but the page does not wait for it. A call that finishes in time behaves exactly as before: its exceptions are re-raised, a missing price still raises, and a slow took_ms still produces the slow_call words. The existing tests still describe the code as written, including test_a_slow_answer_is_still_a_price, because their fakes return straight away and only report a large took_ms.

src/io_shop/account_page.py is unchanged. It already catches PricingServiceFailed in _the_basket_for and renders the page with pricing_unavailable and pricing_failure. So the page still renders when io-pricing is slow, now without the basket total. With the limit in place, a slowdown at io-pricing should add at most about 500ms to the page and no longer pushes the page's latency up to match io-pricing's.

The tests: the new tests in tests/io_shop/test_pricing_service.py use a fake service that actually blocks until the test releases it. They check two things. When the service hangs, basket_total raises PricingServiceFailed naming the host, and it returns within a bound well below the stall. A call that answers within its budget is still a price. Against the old code, the first test would wait on the stalled fake rather than return within the bound. The new test in tests/io_shop/test_account_page.py checks that a page whose pricing service hangs still renders, with its figure and card, the unavailable message and a failure naming io-pricing, within the same kind of bound.

The 500ms limit is a judgement call (SLOW_CALL_MS is 200), and checkout-platform may want to tune it.
How the code outside Code-Fix's patch uses what it changes, read on main
U1 | basket_total at src/io_shop/account_page.py:183, in _the_basket_for: calls it: return basket_total(shopper_id, ask_the_pricing_service), None
Assumptions
- Exchange rate: EUR converted at 0.92191 per USD, published 2026-11-10
- No engineer minutes: no on-call incident was linked to this one, so nobody was paged to respond

Review checklist
✓ Key incident data collected (met)
✓ Impact assessed (met)
○ Root-cause analysis complete (for a person)
  running the proposed fix's tests against the current code would confirm the reading, not that the code it reads is what ran (AI-2)
○ Every action item owned and dated (for a person)
○ Reviewed and shared (for a person)

The document, by field:
overview: For {duration}, io-shop pages loaded slowly for shoppers who used the account page. The account page waits for a separate pricing service to work out each shopper's basket total, and it likely has no time limit on that wait. When the pricing service slowed down, the page slowed down with it, even though it could have been shown without the total. Argus estimates the cost to the shop in lost takings at {customer_loss}. Nobody was paged, so no on-call staff were called out. To end the incident, Argus restarted the pricing service, and that step was confirmed. Argus has also proposed a longer-term fix. It is still a draft and has not been put in place.

Not to be judged:
  - Names in braces, such as {duration}, are figures code writes in from the list of figures in the ask. They are not judged.
  - The overview is written in plain words for the people who lead the company. A claim said more plainly than the postmortem says it is grounded where it means the same.

Judge every claim in the document, and answer by calling judge_claims.

tools.description: Submit every claim in the document, each either as supported or as flagged. Supported: the document's own words, quoted exactly, and the record's rows that support it. Flagged: the document's own words, quoted exactly, why, and the record's rows that contradict it (none where no row speaks to it at all). Empty lists say the document makes no claim to judge.

why.description: One sentence: what the record holds instead. Never empty.
